senses: Someone who sports something.
One who sports or plays with something; a trifler.
examples: But today, the mustache cannot shake its ties to the sexy-yet-buffoonish machismo of the mid-1970s, epitomized by Burt Reynolds, Sam Elliott and the Village People, 'stache sporters all.
We have, however, good reason to suspect the Legislature will soon adopt means of rewarding the ingenuity of these indirect sporters with human life.

senses: Any substance that causes an immune reaction.
Not suitable for breathing.
Not letting air seep through.
examples: The atmosphere on Venus is an unbreathable mixture of carbon dioxide and sulphuric acid, amongst other things.
The air was not just thick, it was unbreathable.

senses: Soft down or fine hair, specifically that covering the human foetus or a tumorous area.
The opposition to political influence of clerics.
A flavored frozen drink made with ice crystals.
A unit of land area equivalent to 3,929 square meters.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish cuerda. Doublet of chord and cord.

senses: Synonym of household goods.
A device for transferring a person with serious mobility issues to and from the floor, a mobility device (such as a wheelchair), seating, and a bed.
ety: After Ted Hoyer, a quadriplegic, who co-invented the device.
examples: St. Luke’s has two types of hoyers that consist of a fabric sling that is placed underneath the patient’s body and an aluminum lift that picks them up. One of the hoyer lifts is electric, while the other is manual.
The disease has affected his legs and arms, and he needs a caregiver at all times, he said. His family uses a hoyer lift to transfer him from his bed to his wheelchair and vice versa.

senses: Synonym of glycerol
ety: From glyco- + -ine, from French glycérine, from Ancient Greek γλυκερός (glukerós, “sweet”) (compare γλυκύς (glukús, “sweet”)).

senses: Synonym of medio, particularly in Asturias, a traditional Spanish unit of dry measure equivalent to about 2.3 L
ety: From Asturian Spanish copín, variant of copino, from copa + -ino.

senses: A translucent, reddish type of zircon used as a gemstone; a hyacinth.
ety: From Middle English jacynct, partly from Old French jacincte, and partly from Old English iacinþ, both from Medieval Latin jacintus, jacinthus, from Latin hyacinthus, from Ancient Greek ὑάκινθος (huákinthos). Doublet of hyacinth.

senses: A combination quesadilla and burrito.
To perform a sonogram upon.
ety: From Latin sonus (“sound”) + -gram, equivalent to sono- + -gram.

senses: A section of verse concerning a single theme; tirade.
ety: Borrowed from French laisse. Doublet of leash.

senses: A cunningly vicious, wild or unmanageable horse.
A woman whose wealth is greater than one million dollars, or the local currency; a female millionaire.
An expert in the science of oenology.
Liable to destruction; capable of being destroyed.
To furnish or fill with men; man.
ety: From Middle English bemannen, bimannen, bemonnen, equivalent to be- + man. Cognate with Middle High German bemannen.
examples: Now do so well as to fare to meet me at thine earliest, and as much bemanned as may be; and let us be both together whatever may happen.

senses: That imprecates or invokes evil.
A col, a lower neck or ridge between two peaks: a mountain pass.
ety: A variant, like hawse (“part of a vessel's bow containing hawseholes”), of Middle English halse (“neck”); see hawse for more.

senses: A French nursemaid.
A soldier armed with a pike.
A person who operates a turnpike.
A miner who works with a pick.
ety: From pike + -man. Compare the Middle English surname Pykeman.

senses: A crab in the act of casting its shell, or immediately afterwards while still soft.
ety: From Middle English schedere (“killer”); equivalent to shed + -er.

senses: The state or quality of being interior.
The state or quality of being private.
An instrument used to detect and measure fluorescence.
A form of medicine to be taken orally, with a one-piece gelatin-based shell around a liquid filling.
An ancient small boat made of wickerwork covered with a hide or leather.
ety: From Latin carabus. The entomological sense is borrowed from translingual Carabus, from the same Latin source.

senses: A subdivision of currency, equal to one hundredth of a Indian, Nepalese, or Pakistani rupee.
A subdivision of currency, equal to one hundredth of a Bangladeshi taka.
A subdivision of currency, equal to one thousandth of an Omani rial.
A subdivision of various former currencies of India.
ety: From Hindi पैसा (paisā) / Urdu پَیسَہ (paisa), from Sauraseni Prakrit *𑀧𑀬𑀁𑀲 (*payaṃsa), presumably from unattested Sanskrit *पदांश (*padāṃśa), from पद (pada, “quarter”) + अंश (aṃśa, “part, piece”) in reference its historical value of ¹⁄₄ anna.

senses: The fourth (wandering ascetic) ashrama in Hindu spiritual life.
A glamorous, important spy.
examples: Well, at least they look good, especially after escaping from the clutches of the superspy baddies.

senses: Covered in blotches.

An apparatus used to perform gasification.

Someone who operates a fly system in a theatre.

Derrick gave his small portmanteau to the flyman and told him to drive there, and he himself set out walking.

senses: An ancient Egyptian musical instrument, to be shaken, consisting of a metal frame holding percussive metal beads.
ety: Borrowed from Latin sīstrum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek σεῖστρον (seîstron), from σείω (seíō, “shake”).

senses: A low-mounted plumbing fixture or type of sink intended for washing the external genitalia and the anus.
Any strain of flu that spreads unusually quickly, is unusually virulent, or is unusually unresponsive to treatment.
examples: In the wake of the superflus and cataclysmic events, male writers tend to jump to that unholy trinity of rape, murder and cannibalism.
